results.claim: In the ordinary Torus Puzzle, where either direction of every unit push is available, SwapPairs applies an involution with k transpositions to a specified b-cell row in exactly 3b+3k pushes, shifts the off-row bodies of the same k auxiliary columns by one chosen step, and fixes every other position; the transposed statement holds for columns.
results.proof_sketch: SwapPairs has three phases, each making one complete tour of the selected row, for 3b row pushes. Each of its k auxiliary columns is moved once per phase. In the source's restricted one-direction model, an inverse column step is simulated by a−1 forward steps. For the ordinary push number the opposite direction is directly available, so each such inverse is one unit push and the three phases use exactly 3k column pushes. Replacing a−1 forward shifts by one inverse shift preserves the positional action: the selected pairs are exchanged, every chosen auxiliary body receives the prescribed one-step cyclic shift, and all other positions return. Cyclic relabeling handles any selected row.

results.claim: On an a×b board with a,b≥2, every even permutation of one specified row is realizable in at most 9b unit pushes while fixing every other position; every even permutation of one specified column is realizable in at most 9a. If a or b is even, every permutation of one specified row or column is realizable in O(a+b) pushes while fixing all other positions.
results.proof_sketch:
Factor an even row permutation π as π=συ, where σ and υ are involutions with the same number k≤b/2 of transpositions. Apply the preceding gadget to σ and υ using the same auxiliary columns and opposite body-shift directions. The side effects cancel and the cost is 2(3b+3k)≤9b. Transposition gives the column bound.

For an odd line permutation, first factor off any fixed adjacent transposition h. If the line length is even, one unit rotation of that line is odd, so h, and hence the original odd permutation, reduces to the even case in O(line length). If the line length is odd, the perpendicular dimension is even. One SwapPairs call performs h but leaves a cycle on the perpendicular line's off-line body. That body has odd length, so its cycle is even and its inverse is performed by the even-column or even-row construction. The total is O(a+b).

results.claim: Two equal adjacent transpositions on rows r<s can be performed exactly in 8(s−r) pushes; the analogous claim holds for columns. A horizontal and a vertical adjacent transposition sharing one cell can be performed in four pushes.
results.proof_sketch: A row-column commutator R C R^{-1} C^{-1}, or its inverse, is a 3-cycle on three L-shaped cells and fixes every other cell. For the four corners x,y,z,w of a 2×2 rectangle, with x,y above z,w, the left-to-right identity (x y z)(x w z)=(x y)(z w) expresses the two horizontal transpositions as two such commutators, costing eight pushes. Chaining the adjacent-row identities from r to s cancels every intermediate transposition and leaves only those on rows r and s. If several residual pairs are formed by pairing consecutive selected rows in sorted order, the total chain length is at most a; similarly it is at most b for columns. Two adjacent perpendicular transpositions sharing their corner compose directly to one of the commutator 3-cycles.

results.claim: A layer consisting of an independent permutation in every row, or in every column, can be performed in O(ab) pushes whenever its global permutation is even. If at least one board dimension is even, an arbitrary row layer or column layer can be performed in O(ab) pushes.
results.proof_sketch: Consider a row layer. For each odd row permutation π_i choose the same adjacent transposition h_i and write π_i=e_i h_i with e_i even. Perform every e_i and every originally even row permutation by the exact even-line construction. Their total cost is O(a·b). If the layer is even, the number of residual h_i is even. Pair consecutive affected rows and use the preceding chains; their total cost is O(a). If the layer is odd but a or b is even, pair all but one residual and perform the remaining transposition by the O(a+b) exact odd-line construction. Since a+b≤ab for a,b≥2, the total remains O(ab). Transposition proves the column-layer statement.

results.claim: Under the structured hypothesis of the audited parent—every non-buffer token is in its target row and all target-column-1 tokens occupy column 1—every sortable board can be completed in O(mn) pushes.
results.proof_sketch: The required correction is a permutation β of column 1 followed by one row layer Π. If a dimension is even, the arbitrary column and row-layer constructions give O(mn). On an odd×odd board, sortability implies sign(β)sign(Π)=+1. If both are even, use the even-layer constructions. If both are odd, factor β=V E_C with V an adjacent vertical transposition, and Π=E_R H with H an adjacent horizontal transposition chosen to share a cell with V. The even column and row parts cost O(mn), while VH is one four-push L-cycle. This strengthens the parent's O(mN) completion to O(N).

results.claim: Every permutation P of the positions of an a×b board has a constructive row-column-row factorization P=A B C, where A and C independently permute positions inside rows and B independently permutes positions inside columns.
results.proof_sketch: Make a bipartite multigraph whose left vertices are current rows and whose right vertices are target rows, with one edge for each token. Both sides have degree b. For any set X of left vertices, the nb-style degree count b|X|≤b|Γ(X)| gives Hall's condition, so the graph has a perfect matching. Removing a perfect matching preserves regularity; repeating decomposes all edges into b perfect matchings, used as intermediate-column colors. First permute each current row so that every token occupies its color column. Each column then contains exactly one token for each target row, so independently permute columns to put tokens in those rows. Finally permute each row into target-column order. Perfect matchings can be found constructively by augmenting paths.

results.claim: For a,b≥2, every position permutation is realizable in O(ab) unit pushes if a or b is even, while every even position permutation is realizable in O(ab) pushes if both dimensions are odd.
results.proof_sketch:
Take P=A B C from the row-column-row factorization. If a or b is even, each of the three arbitrary layers costs O(ab).

Suppose a and b are odd and P is even. Let p_A,p_B,p_C be the layer parities. Their sum is even. If all layers are even, realize them separately. If A and B are odd, select an odd row and an odd column and factor A=E_A H and B=V E_B, where E_A,E_B are even layers and H,V are adjacent transpositions sharing their intersection. Then P=E_A(HV)E_BC, and HV is one four-push L-cycle. The case where B and C are odd is symmetric.

The only separated pattern is A,C odd and B even. Let S swap two columns simultaneously in every row. Since a is odd, S is odd. Replace the factorization by A'=AS, B'=S^{-1}BS, C'=S^{-1}C. These remain row, column, and row layers, their product remains P, conjugation preserves the parity of B, and the parities of A and C both become even. Thus all cases cost O(ab).

results.claim: Every instance A has pn(A)≥ceil(H(A)/n)+ceil(V(A)/m). A global translation by a columns and b rows has exact push number m·d_n(a)+n·d_m(b), where d_k(z)=min(z mod k,k−(z mod k)).
results.proof_sketch: Let H and V sum the cyclic horizontal and vertical distances of all tokens from their targets. A row push moves n tokens by one horizontal edge, so it can reduce H by at most n; column pushes do not change H. Thus at least ceil(H/n) row pushes are necessary. Symmetrically at least ceil(V/m) column pushes are necessary, and the two move counts add. For a global translation, H=mn·d_n(a) and V=mn·d_m(b), giving the lower bound. Reversing the translation by pushing every row and column in a shortest direction attains it.

results.claim: For all m,n≥1 with N=mn>1, the Torus Puzzle push-number diameter satisfies D(m,n)=Θ(N). More precisely, if m,n≥2 then 2N/3≤D(m,n)≤C N for an absolute constant C, while if min{m,n}=1 then D(m,n)=floor(N/2).
results.proof_sketch:
If a dimension is even, every position permutation has the O(N) construction above. If both dimensions are odd, every push is an even cycle, so every sortable permutation is even and again has the O(N) construction. Reversing the constructed identity-to-instance word sorts the instance with the same number of pushes.

For m,n≥2, translate the sorted board by floor(n/2) columns and floor(m/2) rows. Its exact distance is m floor(n/2)+n floor(m/2). Since floor(k/2)≥k/3 for k≥2, this is at least 2mn/3. In one dimension the only sortable configurations are cyclic shifts of the unique nontrivial line, whose cyclic Cayley-graph diameter is floor(N/2). This proves matching uniform bounds and closes the target gap.

results.claim: Let N=mn, s=min{m,n}, and t=max{m,n}. The audited upper bound D(m,n)=O(N·min{s,log t}) remains valid and is strictly strengthened to D(m,n)=O(N).
results.proof_sketch: The preceding construction gives the stronger linear upper bound directly, without FillColumns, radix sorting, or a width restriction. For m,n≥2, both s and log t are bounded below by positive constants, so the audited bound follows immediately. One-dimensional boards have the exact linear bound stated above.

results.claim: For every fixed s≥2, boards with min{m,n}=s have asymptotically tight push number D(m,n)=Θ(mn).
results.proof_sketch: This is an immediate special case of the unrestricted Θ(mn) theorem. The translated-board family continues to provide an explicit matching lower-bound witness.

results.claim: For m,n≥2, D(m,n)≥ceil(log_{d−1}(1+(d−2)(Q−1)/d)), where d=2(m+n), Q=(mn)! if m or n is even, and Q=(mn)!/2 otherwise.
results.proof_sketch: There are Q sortable configurations by the parity characterization. A geodesic contains no adjacent generator-inverse pair. With d nominal directed push labels, at most 1+d((d−1)^L−1)/(d−2) reduced words have length at most L. Coincident direction labels on length-two lines only make this an overcount. A radius-D ball contains all Q sortable configurations, and rearranging the resulting inequality gives the formula.

results.claim: Global translations are not generally diametral: D(2,3)=7, whereas every translated 2×3 board has distance at most 5.
results.proof_sketch: An independently recreated exact breadth-first search with the seven distinct 2×3 generators reached all 720 states with level sizes [1,7,31,115,274,253,36,3], proving diameter 7. The reversed-row state ((3,2,1),(6,5,4)) lies at level 7. Exhausting the six global translations gives distances [0,2,2,3,5,5], whose maximum is 5.

final_writeup:
The open gap closes in the ordinary Torus Puzzle model: D(m,n)=Θ(mn). The point missed by the audited parent is that the original push number permits both directions of every row and column push. The source's SwapPairs procedure was costed in a stricter model, where an inverse column shift is simulated by a−1 forward shifts. In the ordinary model that inverse is one unit push.

Consequently, SwapPairs applies a k-transposition involution to a selected b-cell row in 3b+3k pushes. Its only side effect is a chosen one-step shift of the bodies of k auxiliary columns. Every even row permutation factors into two involutions with the same k≤b/2; applying their gadgets with opposite side-effect directions cancels everything outside the selected row and costs at most 9b. Even column permutations cost at most 9a by transposition.

Odd line permutations leave only a controlled parity issue. If the line length is even, one unit line rotation is odd and reduces the problem to an even permutation. If the line length is odd but the other dimension is even, a single transposition leaves an even cycle on the odd-sized off-line body of one perpendicular line; the even-line gadget cancels it. Thus one odd line permutation costs O(a+b) whenever a dimension is even.

For batching, a four-push row-column commutator is an exact L-shaped 3-cycle. Two appropriately oriented commutators perform the same adjacent transposition on two adjacent parallel lines. Chaining these gadgets pairs residual transpositions on arbitrary parallel lines. Pairing consecutive affected lines makes the sum of chain lengths at most the number of lines. Hence an even row or column layer—an independent permutation on every parallel line—costs O(ab). When a dimension is even, an arbitrary layer has at most one unpaired odd residual, handled in O(a+b), so it also costs O(ab).

It remains to show that three such layers suffice. Given any desired position permutation, form the b-regular bipartite multigraph between current rows and target rows, with one edge per token. Hall's condition follows by degree counting. Repeatedly remove perfect matchings and use them as b intermediate-column colors. A first row layer puts each token in its color column; a column layer sends it to its target row; a final row layer sends it to its target column. This is a constructive row-column-row factorization P=A B C.

If either dimension is even, all three layers are realizable in O(ab), so every permutation is. Now suppose both dimensions are odd and P is even, as every sortable instance must be. If all three layers are even, perform them separately. If two adjacent layers are odd, factor one residual adjacent transposition from each, choose them to share their row-column intersection, and replace their product by one four-push L-cycle; the remaining layers are even. If the two odd layers are the separated row layers A and C, let S simultaneously swap two columns in every row. Since the number of rows is odd, S is odd. The equal factorization P=(AS)(S^{-1}BS)(S^{-1}C) toggles the parities of A and C while preserving that of B, making all three layers even. This exhausts every parity pattern and proves the O(ab) upper bound.

For the lower bound, the displacement certificate gives an exact value for global translations. Translating by floor(n/2) columns and floor(m/2) rows has distance m floor(n/2)+n floor(m/2)≥2mn/3 when m,n≥2. In one dimension the sortable states form a cycle and the diameter is floor(mn/2). Therefore D(m,n)=Θ(mn) uniformly, fully resolving the stated target.

The audited displacement and counting certificates and the exact value D(2,3)=7 remain valid. The parent's fixed-width theorem and O(N·min{s,log t}) upper bound are strict consequences of the new linear theorem, while its structured completion improves from O(mN) to O(N).
